clue.text: Flowers and colour term background for the pavement artist

parts.note: flags are irises, the yellow flag being a common marsh flower
tone is a painter's word for a shade or tint of colour

explanation.surface: A street artist chooses flowers and a colour scheme for a chalk drawing.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface invites you to read 'background' as part of the painting; it is the paving slab the pavement artist chalks on.
explanation.definitionFit: A pavement artist draws in chalk on the paving slabs, so the slab is the base of the picture.

clue.text: Agitator for hot meals

explanation.surface: A troublemaker who likes spicy food.
explanation.walkthrough: A belligerent person is called this; the literal circus performer swallows flames, which are certainly hot meals.
explanation.definitionFit: A hothead who stirs up conflict is so named, and the circus act puts flaming torches in the mouth.

clue.text: Forger's listening 'post ?

parts.note: reads as a counterfeiter's eavesdropping station, but means the smith's iron block, also a tiny bone in the ear

explanation.surface: A counterfeiter sets up a post for eavesdropping.
explanation.walkthrough: The forger is a blacksmith, not a counterfeiter; the middle-ear bone called the incus is named for the smith's block.
explanation.definitionFit: A blacksmith hammers metal on this iron block, and the incus of the inner ear shares the name.

clue.text: A bit of an arch dog

explanation.surface: A dog with a cunning streak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arch' reads as mischievous; it is the architectural curve. The lowest stone from which an arch rises has this name, as does a spaniel breed.
explanation.definitionFit: The stone where an arch begins its curve is so called, and the springer spaniel is a gun-dog breed.

clue.text: Like Alfred's cakes, Mistress?

explanation.surface: A woman compared to the burnt cakes of King Alfred.
explanation.walkthrough: In English legend King Alfred, hiding from the Danes, let a peasant woman's cakes burn. Mistress Overdone is the bawd in Shakespeare's Measure for Measure.
explanation.definitionFit: Burnt cakes are cooked too long, and Shakespeare named his brothel-keeper with that same word.

clue.text: Can she be made to realize?

indicators.note: the letters of the two words are to be made into another word, a signal to rearrange

explanation.surface: Can a woman be brought to understand?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Realize' looks like understand, but it means convert into money; 'be made' remakes CAN SHE.
explanation.definitionFit: To realize an asset or cheque is to turn it into cash.

clue.text: Relations prayed for by Buzfuz in court

definitions.text: prayed for by Buzfuz in court

explanation.surface: A barrister asks the court to hear from the family of the accused.
explanation.walkthrough: Serjeant Buzfuz is the barrister for the plaintiff in Bardell v Pickwick in Dickens's Pickwick Papers. A 'tales' was a writ summoning extra jurors when too few turned up, and counsel would 'pray a tales'.
explanation.definitionFit: Relations are narratives or stories told; the legal writ named for its Latin opening word calls in bystanders to make up a jury.

clue.text: Vestigial harness?

parts.note: joins remnant marks with the straps by which a horse pulls a cart

explanation.definitionFit: Faint remains are vestiges, and the side straps linking a horse's collar to a carriage share the name.

clue.text: Picture of sand-storm in a strange place

indicators.note: the scrambled sand goes inside the scrambled place
a strange version of the word place is one with its letters altered
a sandstorm whirls grains about, so the letters of sand are tossed into a new order

explanation.surface: A painting shows a sandstorm in an unfamiliar spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sand-storm' reads as one weather word, but 'storm' rearranges SAND to ANDS, which goes 'in' LCAPE, the 'strange' rearrangement of PLACE.
explanation.definitionFit: A landscape is a painting of countryside scenery.

clue.text: 'In which system we are all revolutionaries

definitions.text: In which system we are all revolutionaries

parts.words: In which system we are all revolutionaries
parts.note: sounds like a political regime of rebels, but means the planetary arrangement in which Earth and its people revolve round the Sun

explanation.surface: A political system where everyone is a rebel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionaries' means those who revolve: everyone on Earth circles the Sun.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sun's family of planets is named for the star, and Earth orbits within it.

clue.text: Lakeside cleric's. dream state.

parts.note: Rev is the abbreviation for Reverend, the title of a cleric
Lake Erie, one of the North American Great Lakes, placed at the side of the cleric

explanation.surface: A clergyman sitting by a lake drifts into a daydream.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lakeside' does double duty only in the surface: it gives the lake, ERIE, and tells you it sits beside the cleric.
explanation.definitionFit: A reverie is a daydream, a state of being lost in pleasant thoughts.

clue.text: A way to negotiate for entry into Europe

definitions.text: A way to negotiate for entry into Europe

parts.words: A way to negotiate for entry into Europe
parts.note: reads like a diplomat's route into the Common Market, but means a course or route, and also the strait crossed from Britain to the Continent

explanation.surface: Britain looks for a diplomatic route into the European community.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Negotiate' means bargain in the surface, but here it means get across, as one negotiates an obstacle; the English Channel lies between Britain and France.
explanation.definitionFit: A channel is a route or means of communication, and the stretch of sea separating England from France must be crossed to reach mainland Europe.

clue.text: Find the Lady? Measure and take two from the end

parts.note: an ell is an old measure of cloth length, about 45 inches

indicators.note: keep only the opening two letters of the following word, end

explanation.surface: A card-sharp's game of Find the Lady, followed by instructions for measuring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Find the Lady' is the three-card trick; here it only points to a woman's name. Two letters from 'end' give EN.
explanation.definitionFit: Ellen is a woman's given name, so it names a lady.

clue.text: Lady poet in the apo'he cary's shop

parts.note: Di is a short form of the woman's name Diana
Edmund Spenser, Elizabethan poet who wrote The Faerie Queene

explanation.surface: A female poet is found working in a chemist's shop.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition describes the person you would find in a pharmacy making up medicines.
explanation.definitionFit: A dispenser is a pharmacist's assistant who prepares and hands out medicines in a chemist's shop.

clue.text: A price on, one's head at leap-frog

explanation.surface: Someone has a bounty set on their head during a playground game.
explanation.walkthrough: In British children's leapfrog the call was 'tuck in your twopenny', meaning your head; a twopenny item also costs two pence.
explanation.definitionFit: Two old British pence is a small cost; in schoolyard slang the word also meant the head you keep low while others vault over.

clue.text: " An only father, Sir, might expect more" (Goldsmith)

definitions.text: " An only father, Sir, might expect more" (Goldsmith)

parts.words: " An only father, Sir, might expect more" (Goldsmith)
parts.note: a quotation from Oliver Goldsmith with its last word missing, what a father hopes for from his child

explanation.surface: A line from Goldsmith about a father's hopes, with a word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue is a fill-in-the-blank quotation from Oliver Goldsmith; the missing word is what a parent expects from a child.
explanation.definitionFit: A father expects dutiful compliance from his children.

clue.text: How to come clean, if one's first excuse will not ?

definitions.text: if one's first excuse will not

explanation.surface: Advice on confessing when your first alibi fails.
explanation.walkthrough: An excuse that 'won't wash' is not believed; to come clean in the literal sense you bathe.
explanation.definitionFit: Bathing is how you get physically clean, and an excuse that does not convince is said not to do this.

clue.text: Sporting equalizers

parts.note: not goals that level the score, but the weights or strokes given to stronger competitors to even out a contest

explanation.definitionFit: In golf and horse racing, extra weight or stroke allowances level the chances of unequal competitors.

clue.text: Liberal whose actions prove him so?

explanation.surface: A Liberal politician whose deeds show what he is.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'handsome is as handsome does' says good looks are proved by good deeds; 'Liberal' means generous, not the party.
explanation.definitionFit: A generous gift is described this way, and the proverb says good conduct shows true good looks.

clue.text: Outsider of the Apollo mission.?

explanation.surface: Someone excluded from the Apollo moon mission.
explanation.walkthrough: An outsider is an unlikely winner in racing; a shot fired all the way to the Moon is a distant one.
explanation.definitionFit: A rank outsider in betting is a bet with little chance, and a Moon rocket is literally a very distant launch.

clue.text: Cotton's drum ?

parts.note: a cylinder on which sewing thread is wound, with drum read as a spool rather than a percussion instrument

explanation.definitionFit: Sewing thread is sold wound on a small spool or bobbin.

clue.text: Old gold lost at Waterloo:

explanation.surface: Treasure that went missing on a famous battlefield.
explanation.walkthrough: A napoleon was a twenty-franc French gold coin; the emperor was defeated at Waterloo in 1815.
explanation.definitionFit: The French gold coin bore the emperor's name, and the emperor was the loser of the 1815 battle.

clue.text: Some seem to jump right into the heavens

indicators.note: the letter for right goes into the word for the heavens

parts.note: the skies are the heavens above

explanation.surface: Some people appear to leap straight up into the sky.
explanation.walkthrough: Ski jumpers seem to leap into the sky; 'into' puts R inside SKIES.
explanation.definitionFit: Ski jumpers are winter sportspeople who fly off a ramp.

clue.text: Swift nickname is something to conjure with

explanation.surface: A fast nickname that a magician might use.
explanation.walkthrough: Jonathan Swift, author of Gulliver's Travels, was nicknamed this by the Duchess of Shrewsbury; magicians say 'hey' before it.
explanation.definitionFit: The Irish satirist was given this nickname, and conjurors use the word as they produce a trick.

clue.text: Performed like old movies .. before they went out

explanation.surface: Old films were shown before people went out for the evening.
explanation.walkthrough: Early films jerked and shimmered on screen, hence 'the flicks'; candles waver before going out.
explanation.definitionFit: Early cinema images wavered unsteadily, and a dying flame wavers just before it is extinguished.

clue.text: How some go ahead to make money

explanation.surface: How ambitious people get on and earn money.
explanation.walkthrough: You 'forge ahead' when making steady progress; counterfeiters make money in a different way.
explanation.definitionFit: One presses on in this way, and counterfeiters fake banknotes by doing the same.

clue.text: Gin that is mixed to make other spirits

indicators.note: the letters of gin and the abbreviation are blended like a cocktail into a new order

parts.note: i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, meaning that is

explanation.surface: Gin mixed into cocktails produces other drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spirits' means drinks in the surface but supernatural beings in the definition. 'mixed' rearranges GIN plus IE.
explanation.definitionFit: Genies (singular genie or genius) are spirits of Arabian folklore, quite unlike drinking spirits.

clue.text: In. Spain a director finds the lowest point.

annotationWithheld.why: In Spain a director finds the lowest point (5): A DIR(ector) gives ADIR, but no reading of 'In Spain' supplies the opening N.
annotationWithheld.clue: In. Spain a director finds the lowest point.

clue.text: Forest officers shooting in Glasgow

explanation.surface: Foresters go out shooting in a Scottish city.
explanation.walkthrough: Rangers is a Glasgow football club; its players shoot at goal.
explanation.definitionFit: Park and forest wardens are known by this title, which is also the name of a famous Glasgow football team.

clue.text: A class some' of whom may be charmed to perform

definitions.text: A class some' of whom may be charmed to perform

parts.words: A class some' of whom may be charmed to perform
parts.note: suggests pupils in a school class won over to act, but means a zoological group whose members sway for a snake charmer

explanation.surface: Some pupils in a class can be coaxed into putting on a show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Class' is the zoological rank; snake charmers make cobras rise from a basket.
explanation.definitionFit: Ophidia is the zoological name for snakes, and cobras are the creatures charmers coax from baskets.

clue.text: 50-50, or 7 perhaps

indicators.note: suggests the spelt-out number could be arranged differently, so its letters are reshuffled

parts.note: the number seven written out as a word

explanation.surface: An even chance, or maybe the number seven.
explanation.walkthrough: 7 looks odd beside 'evens', but it is spelt out as SEVEN and 'perhaps' rearranges its letters.
explanation.definitionFit: In betting, odds of one to one mean an equal chance of winning or losing.

clue.text: Upsets public vessels

parts.note: overt means open, done in public view
urns are vases or containers

explanation.surface: Containers on public view get knocked over.
explanation.definitionFit: To upset something is to tip it over, as a capsizing boat does.
